name: 'Experience' and its limits
plain_explanation: Russell asks what actually distinguishes an experienced event from an unexperienced one, concluding that experience requires life and, more specifically, that an event is 'experienced' when it sets up a habit (memory being one kind of habit).
precise_definition: Russell's own supplementary analysis, offered in assessing James's use of 'experience': there is no experience except where there is life, but experience is not coextensive with life either, since many things happen to an organism without being noticed; an event may be said to be 'experienced' when it sets up a habit, habits being possible only in living organisms (illustrated by the burnt child who fears fire even without explicit memory of being burnt).
why_it_mattered: It grounds Russell's sole substantive disagreement with James's radical empiricism, and shows why Russell thinks 'pure experience' cannot, after all, be identified with the single 'stuff' of the whole world.
examples: Rain falling in an uninhabited desert is not experienced, though rain seen or felt to fall is.
A burnt poker does not fear the fire, however often it is heated, because it cannot form habits.
